title: Video2GUI: Synthesizing Large-Scale Interaction Trajectories for Generalized GUI Agent Pretraining
claim: A raw, unlabeled data source is turned into grounded training data by a staged pipeline of filtering, extraction and grounding.
layout: 3 panels (A top, B and C bottom), left-to-right flow, dashed boxes
description: The figure is a three-part pipeline drawn in dashed blue rounded boxes. Panel A spans the top and is titled Coarse-to-Fine Video Filtering. It runs left to right with large icons: a cluster of raw internet videos (500M+), then meta-info filtering (a document with a gear), then candidate videos (~20M), then video quality scoring (an eye and film frame with speech bubbles for instruction clarity, topic relevance and recording quality), and finally a stack of high-quality tutorial videos (4.2M, 300k hours). Panel B, bottom left, is Trajectory Extraction. A film strip of screenshots S1 to SM feeds a Gemini-3-Pro robot icon, which outputs a text card with the task instruction and a timestamped action trajectory. Panel C, bottom right, is Action Spatial Grounding. Three frames (o_t-0.5s, o_t, o_t+0.5s) feed a second robot icon, which outputs a screenshot with a red bounding box and the coordinates b_t = (x1,y1,x2,y2). Big blue arrows guide the eye, and the eye lands first on the icon-rich top row.
caption: Overview of the VideoGUI pipeline. VideoGUI consists of three stages: (A) coarse-to-fine video filtering for selecting high-quality tutorial videos, (B) trajectory extraction that converts video segments into instruction–trajectories sequences, and (C) action spatial grounding that maps low-level instructions to precise UI targets to produce grounded trajectories.
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have driven growing interest in graphical user interface (GUI) agents, yet their generalization remains constrained by the scarcity of large-scale training data spanning diverse real-world applications. Existing datasets rely heavily on costly manual annotations and are typically confined to narrow domains. To address this challenge, we propose Video2GUI, a fully automated framework that extracts grounded GUI interaction trajectories directly from unlabeled Internet videos. Video2GUI employs a coarse-to-fine filtering strategy to identify high-quality GUI tutorial videos and convert them into structured agent trajectories. Applying this pipeline to 500 million video metadata entries, we construct WildGUI, a large-scale dataset containing 12 million interaction trajectories spanning over 1,500 applications and websites. Pre-training Qwen2.5-VL and Mimo-VL on WildGUI yields consistent improvements of 5-20% across multiple GUI grounding and action benchmarks, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. We will release both the WildGUI dataset and the Video2GUI pipeline to support future research of GUI agents.
